plan.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect, from the US prescribing information (rev 7/2026) and Medication Guide only. Fixed resubmission of the verified script held on 11-11 and given a REVISE on 11-20 and 11-21 (playbook queue #4). It is not a duplicate of a live video; check the live list first.
plan.angle: Locked label-only script with every fix applied. s28: 10.3% stopped because of adverse events vs 2.7% on placebo (not 2.6%). s42: the Medication Guide's pancreatitis wording exactly ('with or without vomiting', no 'nausea'). s54: drop 'is requiring' and keep the FDA's 'potential' increased risk for NAION, crediting the 9 Nov 2026 FDA Drug Safety Communication unless the live PI prints it. Keep the 11-20 fixes: 'didn't stop because of adverse events', 'adverse events' never 'side effects', 'weight-related', and 'the label's Trial 1, in adults without diabetes', with the label's top dose giving -11.1% (any 36 mg / -11.2% figure is labelled as trial-only). Add the drug, timeframe and measure on the s31 and s32 cards, and 'your own history of MTC or MEN 2'. Opening: sentence 1 names orforglipron and the question. Never open with a 'Short answer.' label. Sentence 2 is one concrete thing the viewer may feel (food may sit longer, mild queasiness mostly during dose escalation that decreased over time), then the number. Render fixes: masking 0.02 or lower, a full description ending '…whether it's right for you.', and consistent character design between shots. Include the Health Canada and TGA line only if the regulators' own pages confirm both dates. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Publisher: put a ▶ Watch next link to How It Works after the first paragraph.
plan.why: Playbook priority #1: an approved, searched drug name ('foundayo' already brings us 476 lifetime minutes), Foundayo Shorts are spiking (826 views on day 1), and Australia, Canada and the UK launched it this week. The body rests on settled label evidence.

package.description:
Safety: Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without nausea or vomiting? Stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't one of the emergency signs in the video, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Starting orforglipron, the Foundayo pill? You may feel full sooner, and queasy mostly while doses step up.

Quick answer: In the label's Trial 1, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, average weight loss on the label's top dose of orforglipron (Foundayo) was 11.1% at 72 weeks vs 2.1% on placebo. Across the label's two trials (Trial 2 was in adults with type 2 diabetes), about 10% on the top dose stopped because of adverse reactions, vs about 3% on placebo. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common while the dose was being increased, and decreased over time.

Sources:
1. FOUNDAYO (orforglipron) US Prescribing Information and Medication Guide, rev 7/2026 - https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html
2. NHS, Feeling sick (nausea), last reviewed 17 Nov 2023 - https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/feeling-sick-nausea/

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
package.pinned_comment: The label's Trial 1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes): average weight loss on orforglipron's top dose was 11.1% at 72 weeks vs 2.1% on placebo. Across the label's two trials (Trial 2 was in adults with type 2 diabetes), about 10% on the top dose stopped because of adverse reactions, vs about 3% on placebo. The label says don't take it if you or anyone in your family has had a thyroid cancer called MTC, or if you have an inherited condition called MEN 2. For anything that isn't one of the emergency signs in the video, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Save this for your first weeks. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

visual.stat_label: Avg loss, top dose; placebo −2.1%, 72 wks

scenes.retention_device: Headline number with its comparator delivered by ~15 s

scenes.narration: That's from the label's Trial 1, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. And that early queasiness? The label says it decreased over time.
scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff inside 30 s, with the full trial population in the same sentence

scenes.narration: Later, I'll show you the number most people skip: how many stopped because of adverse reactions, and what that means for your first months.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (one sentence), paid off in 'What the trial showed'

scenes.narration: First, who it's for. Then the first weeks, and the signs that mean call right away.
So who is the Foundayo pill actually for?
In the US, it's approved for chronic weight management, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.

visual.stock_query: pill beside healthy plate, walking shoes

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the chapter question, under 70 s

scenes.narration: That means adults with obesity, or adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related condition.
scenes.retention_device: Viewer checks themselves against the list

scenes.narration: It's one pill, once a day. No injection, no pen to learn.
And it isn't the semaglutide pill. Orforglipron is a small molecule, not a peptide, built to switch on the same GLP-1 receptor your gut hormone uses.

visual.fact: Orforglipron: a small molecule, same GLP-1 receptor

scenes.retention_device: Myth flip: corrects a common mix-up

scenes.narration: Your label spells out exactly when and how to take it, so go through those directions with your pharmacist on day one.
But here's the part to check before day one. Who shouldn't take it?
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook question before the safety detail

scenes.narration: The label says don't take it if you or anyone in your family has had a thyroid cancer called MTC, or if you have an inherited condition called MEN 2.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete check the viewer can act on

scenes.narration: That comes from the label's boxed warning. Thyroid C-cell tumors were seen in rodents given other GLP-1 medicines. Orforglipron doesn't act in rodents, and no tumors were seen with it there. Whether this matters in people hasn't been determined.
scenes.on_screen_text: Class rodent finding; human relevance not determined

scenes.narration: It's also not for anyone who's had a serious allergic reaction to orforglipron or any of its ingredients.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not with a serious allergy to it

scenes.narration: And tell your prescriber about a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing or shortness of breath. Those are the thyroid signs the Medication Guide lists.

items: Trouble swallowing or short of breath

scenes.retention_device: Sign plus action in one beat

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, forty-eight, picking up her first prescription. She's cleared those questions with her doctor. Her real worry? Feeling sick at her desk in week two.
scenes.retention_device: Introduces the hypothetical thread and a mini-cliffhanger into the next chapter

scenes.narration: So what do the first weeks actually feel like?
You start on a low dose, and your prescriber steps it up gradually. The label builds in that slow climb, and it matters for your stomach.
Your prescriber sets those steps, not a chart online. If a step feels rough, that's a conversation, not a failure.
scenes.on_screen_text: A rough step? Talk, don't tough it
scenes.retention_device: Validation with relief in the same beat

scenes.narration: The most common side effects in the label are stomach ones, like nausea, constipation and diarrhea.
scenes.retention_device: Names what the viewer is worried about

scenes.narration: Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common while the dose was being increased, and they decreased over time. So week two may feel different from month three.
scenes.on_screen_text: Higher during dose steps, then decreased

scenes.narration: Here's what's happening inside. GLP-1 medicines slow how fast your stomach empties, and they act on appetite signals in the brain.
In daily life, you may simply feel full sooner than you're used to.

visual.stock_query: person pushing half plate away, content

scenes.narration: For Dana, that might mean leaving half her lunch. That's okay. Fullness is a signal to stop, not a challenge to finish.
scenes.on_screen_text: Full is a signal, not a challenge

visual.stock_query: Dana at desk, half lunch, smiling

scenes.retention_device: Returns to the thread; removes guilt

scenes.narration: What may help with queasiness? The NHS suggests smaller, more frequent meals, not eating too quickly, and avoiding hot, fried or greasy food.
It also suggests not lying down right after eating, and sipping cold drinks through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids.

visual.stock_query: person sipping cold water on sofa

scenes.narration: One sign never waits, though: severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away. Stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away? Stop it, call right away
scenes.retention_device: Sign and action in one line, not a chapter-ending warning

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your prescriber first.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not that emergency sign? Don't stop or change it on your own

scenes.narration: And if vomiting or diarrhea keeps going, mention it. The label warns that losing fluids this way can lead to kidney problems, so keep drinking, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
scenes.retention_device: Useful safety fact folded into a tip

scenes.narration: So the stomach side was reported mostly early. But the question everyone really wants answered is bigger: how much weight, and how many stayed with it?
So what did the trial actually show?
In the label's Trial 1, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, took it for seventy-two weeks alongside diet and activity.
scenes.retention_device: Population and timeframe in one sentence

scenes.narration: On the top dose, average weight loss was eleven point one percent. On placebo, it was two point one percent.

visual.stat_label: Avg weight loss, top dose vs placebo

scenes.retention_device: Callback to the opening number with the comparator

scenes.narration: Our own arithmetic: starting at two hundred pounds, that average is about twenty-two pounds. Starting at ninety kilos, about ten.
But it's an average, so your own result could land above or below it.
Lower doses brought less weight loss on average. That's one reason the dose steps are your prescriber's call.
scenes.retention_device: New fact that links back to dose steps

scenes.narration: And weight is only one measure. How you feel, how you move and your other health numbers count too.
Which brings us to the number I promised. The one most people skip. How many people stopped because of adverse reactions?
Across the label's two trials, ten percent on the top dose stopped because of adverse reactions. On placebo, it was three percent. Trial 2 was in adults with type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for adverse reactions, 17.2 mg vs placebo
visual.stock_query: two stat bubbles side by side

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: Flip that around, with our own arithmetic: about nine in ten people on the top dose didn't stop because of adverse reactions.

visual.stat_label: Didn't stop for adverse reactions (our math)

scenes.retention_device: Reframe that relieves, from our own arithmetic

scenes.narration: Some people also stopped for other reasons, so overall dropout was higher than that.
So what does that mean for you? Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common during the dose steps. Tell your prescriber early if side effects get in your way.
And there's a short list of signs that should never wait for your next appointment.
Which signs mean call right away?
First, pancreatitis. The Medication Guide's sign is severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without nausea or vomiting.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away

scenes.narration: If that happens, stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Stop it and call right away

scenes.narration: Second, gallbladder problems: pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools. Tell your healthcare provider right away.
Third, a serious allergic reaction: swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, severe rash or itching, fainting or feeling dizzy, or a very rapid heartbeat.

items: Trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching
Fainting or dizzy; very rapid heartbeat

scenes.retention_device: Third numbered sign, full Medication Guide list

scenes.narration: For any of those, stop taking it and get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Allergy signs: stop it, get help right away

scenes.narration: If you have diabetes and also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, your risk of low blood sugar is higher. The label also reports low blood sugar in adults without type 2 diabetes. Signs include shakiness, sweating, dizziness and confusion.
scenes.on_screen_text: Low blood sugar: higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea

scenes.narration: The FDA has also flagged a potential increased risk of a rare problem with the nerve at the back of the eye, with GLP-1 medicines.
scenes.on_screen_text: FDA: potential rare optic nerve risk
scenes.retention_device: Surprising fact late in the list

scenes.narration: If you notice sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, contact your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Sudden vision loss in one eye? Call right away
scenes.retention_device: Sign plus action in one line

scenes.narration: And before any procedure with anesthesia or deep sedation, tell your care team you take it. The label flags a risk of food or liquid getting into the lungs.
If you're ever unsure whether something counts, calling is never overreacting. That's what your care team is there for.
That's the serious list, and it's short. The rest is the part you control: getting the most from every pill.
So what helps you get the most from it?
Start with the label itself. The approved use pairs the pill with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. That's part of the plan, not fine print.
A simple habit: eat the protein on your plate first, like eggs, fish, beans, yogurt or chicken, so it doesn't get crowded out when you fill up fast.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete tip tied to feeling full sooner

scenes.narration: Then keep your muscles busy. US guidelines suggest muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week.

visual.stat_label: Muscle-strengthening per week, US adult guidelines

scenes.narration: Plus at least a hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity, like brisk walking, across the week.

visual.stat_label: Moderate activity per week, US adults

scenes.narration: Eat slowly, too. The NHS tip for nausea, not eating too quickly, fits right in when you feel full sooner.
Picture Dana at month three. Smaller lunches, protein first, a walk after dinner, two short strength sessions a week. Not perfect. Steady.
And if her scale stalls for a week, she's not failing. She's watching her energy, her strength and how she feels, not just one number.
So here's your Foundayo checklist.
One: go over your history with your prescriber, including your own history of MTC or MEN 2, and any family history of MTC.

items: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea: mostly dose steps

scenes.retention_device: Recap in the label's exact terms

scenes.narration: Two: expect nausea, vomiting or diarrhea mostly during the dose steps, and speak up early if side effects get in your way.
Three: know the call-right-away signs, starting with severe stomach pain that won't go away.
It's a prescription medicine, and this isn't personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask if it's right for you

scenes.narration: If you've felt nervous about starting, knowing what's ahead is how you go in steady instead of scared. You've got this.
If this helped, subscribe for more answers straight from the label and the trials. There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against the live Foundayo label (Revised 7/2026), the FDA safety notice of 9 Nov 2026, the NHS nausea page, the CDC activity page and the PubMed entry for the NEJM paper. Every number checks out. Trial 1 ran 72 weeks in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes. Weight change was −11.1% on 17.2 mg vs −2.1% on placebo, and lower doses lost less (−7.4% and −8.3%). Pooled across Trials 1 and 2, 10% on 17.2 mg stopped because of adverse reactions vs 3% on placebo. The boxed warning wording is right: orforglipron isn't active in rats or mice and didn't cause tumors in them. The MTC/MEN 2 rules, the gallbladder signs, the full allergy-sign list, low blood sugar in adults without type 2 diabetes, the kidney and aspiration warnings, and the statement that nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time all match the label. The FDA notice covers orforglipron. Our own arithmetic is labelled as ours and is correct (≈22 lb from 200 lb; ≈10 kg from 90 kg). The safety lines, the 'talk to your doctor or prescriber' line and the Dana scenario are fine.

Note on s46: Foundayo's own Medication Guide says 'with or without nausea or vomiting'. So the line is correct for this label, even though our craft notes (written for another label's wording) say never to add 'nausea'. Keep it as written.

Only small wording fixes remain: a few places say 'mostly' where the label says 'higher during dose escalation', one line suggests all the most common side effects are stomach ones, and s07 doesn't use the label's indication wording.

issues.claim: So the stomach side was reported mostly early.
issues.problem: The label says nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time. It doesn't say they were reported 'mostly' early. That's a slightly stronger claim than the source makes.
issues.fix: So stomach effects were more common during the dose steps, then decreased. But the question everyone really wants answered is bigger: how much weight, and how many stayed with it?

issues.claim: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea: mostly dose steps / expect nausea, vomiting or diarrhea mostly during the dose steps
issues.problem: The recap adds 'mostly' and drops the label's wording ('higher during dose escalation… decreased over time').
issues.fix: s66 list item: "Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea: higher during dose steps". s67 narration: "Two: nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common during the dose steps and decreased over time, so speak up early if side effects get in your way."

issues.claim: You may feel full sooner, and queasy mostly while doses step up.
issues.problem: Same 'mostly' issue as s31 and s66–s67.
issues.fix: You may feel full sooner, and queasy more often while doses step up.

issues.claim: The most common side effects in the label are stomach ones, like nausea, constipation and diarrhea.
issues.problem: The label's list of most common adverse reactions also includes headache, fatigue and hair loss. As written, the line suggests they are all stomach effects.
issues.fix: Narration: "The most common side effects in the label are mostly stomach ones, like nausea, constipation and diarrhea." On-screen: "Most common: mostly stomach effects"

issues.problem: The label's indication is 'to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term'. 'Chronic weight management' is fine as a paraphrase but isn't the label's wording.
issues.fix: Narration: "In the US, it's approved to reduce excess body weight and keep it off long term, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity." On-screen: "US: weight reduction + long-term maintenance"

thumbnail.reasoning: #0 ("QUEASY? NORMAL?") pairs a clearly worried face with a felt, specific symptom a new starter would search for, names the drug in the subtext ("STARTING THE FOUNDAYO PILL"), and leaves the actual answer (that GI effects are mostly during dose escalation) for the video — strong curiosity gap, matching emotion-to-text, and it mirrors the studio's best-performing prior pattern. Text is legible at both 240px and 168px sizes with only two short lines. #1's "11.1%" is a strong, credible stat hook and legible, but it partially front-loads the headline answer (the weight-loss number itself) even though the video covers more ground, slightly softening curiosity. #2 is clean and legible but generic — "YOUR FIRST WEEKS?" could apply to any medication, it never names the drug in the subtext (violating the house rule), and the before/after faces are a weaker, less specific emotional hook than a named symptom. All three clear the legibility bar, but #0 offers the best mix of specificity, emotional match, and open curiosity without revealing the payoff.

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The facts and packaging are sound: both checks passed with only minor wording notes, and the label's "with or without nausea or vomiting" wording is correct for Foundayo. But the render is broken. The closing scene (the subscribe ask and the watch-next line) has no voice at all while its captions still run, and the masking is 0.021, over the 0.02 limit. Both are ship-blockers, so regenerate that scene, re-mix to 0.015 or lower, apply the minor "mostly" and s21 wording fixes and resubmit quickly while the Foundayo Short is still getting views.
